pages.text:
*Way to Lose #13: Have a plan that only works if nobody else is on the field.*

The bus smells like pine cleaner and old bread, a scent that somehow manages to be both refreshing and ancient all at once. Coach Gin does not sit in the driver’s seat; instead, she stands in the aisle, blocking the light, and slides fifty-one paper plates onto the bench in front of us. One plate for every goal we have let in, which is a lot of plates, clicking together like a stack of white teeth.

“Pick one,” she says, her voice flat as a table. “Write down exactly how it happened. No excuses. No feelings. Just facts.”

I pick a plate, then a marker, my hand trembling slightly but refusing to show it, and I write: *Own goal. My foot. My bad.*

Josie is already narrating the scene. “And here we have the evidence,” she whispers loudly, leaning in. “The crime scene. The plate of shame. I am the detective. The duck is the witness.”

Luz, who is sitting on my lap because the seats are too short for her, holds up her crayon notebook and points to a page where she has drawn a very sad duck and the word GOAL in red. “This is evidence,” she says, her face serious. “It proves the duck is guilty.”

Gin looks at Luz, then at me. She does not smile. She does not laugh. She just nods, once, and turns to the next kid.
pages.image: A girl in a yellow armband writes on a white paper plate inside a big blank yellow minibus, surrounded by many other plates, while a small girl in her lap points at a crayon drawing; a tiny girl in a sports band watches from a bench seat.

pages.text:
The plates pile up on the dashboard, a white mountain that looks like it might collapse if you breathed on it too hard. Gin sorts them with quick, precise movements, her hands moving faster than a dealer in a movie who knows they are not being watched.

“Fourteen here,” she says, tapping a neat stack. “Ball rolls left. Slant. Gravity. Parking lot.”

“Seventeen here,” she says, tapping another pile. “Midfield. Lost. Too many touches.”

“Eleven here,” she says, looking directly at Priya. Priya shrinks, pulling her oversized gloves into her lap like a shy turtle. “Goalkeeper. Eyes. Closed.”

Priya looks like she is about to vomit. I want to say something, to explain that it was windy, or that the sun was in her face, or that she is tiny and the ball is big, but Gin does not let me. She puts a single plate in the corner, separate from the rest.

“One here,” she says. “Duck.”

“Which duck?” I ask.

Gin shrugs. “The one that did not give it back.”

Ahmed is fidgeting, picking at a loose thread on his jersey while he looks at the pile of seventeen, then the pile of fourteen, and finally at me.
pages.image: A big blank yellow minibus dashboard covered in stacks of white paper plates; a short woman in a yellow windbreaker points to a stack while a tiny girl in oversized gloves looks down, and a large boy picks at his jersey.

pages.text:
Ahmed stands up, and the bus lurches under his sudden weight. He is the fastest kid in the league, a fact he wears like a badge, proud and slightly smug.

“Passing is slow,” he says, his voice hard as a brick. “I run. I score. That is the game.”

Gin turns to him. She does not raise her voice. She just waits, her steel thermos catching the afternoon light.

“Four goals,” she says softly. “Out of six. You scored them.”

Ahmed nods, crossing his arms over his chest. “See? I am the solution. The rest of them are the problem.”

Gin points to the pile of fifty-one plates, a white mountain that looks like it might collapse if you breathed on it too hard. “How many of these,” she asks, “happened when you were not near the ball?”

Ahmed opens his mouth. He closes it. He looks at the plate in his hand, then at the pile, and finally at me. For the first time, he does not look like he knows the answer. He looks like a guy who just realized he forgot his wallet.
pages.image: A lanky boy stands in the aisle of a big blank yellow minibus with arms crossed, looking down at a white paper plate, while a short woman in sunglasses points to a large stack of plates on the dashboard.

pages.text:
I stand up too, though I cannot explain why. My legs just seem to decide on their own, pushing my chair back with a screech that sounds like a dying goose. “I was there,” I say, and my voice is so loud it bounces off the ceiling tiles. “For the midfield ones. I had the ball. I lost it. It is my fault. It is always my fault.”

Josie stops narrating. She stops talking entirely, which is like watching the sun go out, and she looks at me with her mouth hanging open, waiting for me to stop. But I am not going to stop. I am going to keep going until I am a statue, or a mistake, or a lie.

“I take the shots,” I continue, my chest tight like a shirt that is two sizes too small. “I make the passes. I cover the gaps. I am the captain, which means I carry the weight. If we lose, it is because I did not carry it enough.”

Tank looks at me with wide, worried eyes. He opens his mouth to say sorry, the way he always does, but he doesn’t. He just looks at me, his big hands hovering uselessly in the air.

Gin does not interrupt. She just watches me, her face calm and flat.
pages.image: A girl with a high ponytail and a yellow armband stands up in a big blank yellow minibus aisle, hands clenched, looking angry and scared, while a large gentle boy and a talkative girl watch her from the bench seats.

pages.text:
My chest still feels tight, like I just ran a mile in the wrong shoes. I want to quit. I want to go home and sit in my room and stare at the ceiling until the world fixes itself.

Gin reaches into her pocket. She pulls out a single white plate. It is clean. It is blank.

She writes one word on it in black marker. The letters are thick. They are bold.

She hands it to me.

“Loss Log,” she says. “Make a new page. Call it Strategy Log.”

I take the plate. It is warm from her hand. The word is FIXABLE.

I look at the word. I look at the pile of fifty-one failures. I look at the bus, which is pulling into the park.

I put the plate on the dashboard. It is not a trophy. It is a map.
pages.image: A girl holds a white paper plate with a single word written on it, standing in a big blank yellow minibus, while a short woman in a yellow windbreaker watches her with a calm expression; the big blank yellow minibus is parked near a muddy field.
